questions.q: In crontab syntax, what does 0 2 * * * /opt/scripts/backup.sh schedule?
options: The script runs at 2:00 AM every day
The script runs every 2 minutes
The script runs once, 2 hours after the crontab is saved
The script runs on the 2nd day of every month only
questions.explain: The fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week — 0 and 2 set the time to 2:00 AM, and * in the remaining fields means every day.

questions.q: What extra field does a job in /etc/crontab or /etc/cron.d/ have that a personal crontab -e entry doesn't?
options: The user the job should run as
The server's hostname
An email address for failure notifications
The job's priority level
questions.explain: System-wide cron files have no single personal owner, so each line must explicitly name the user to run the command as.

questions.q: What does Persistent=true do on a systemd timer unit that plain cron cannot replicate?
options: Runs the missed job once the system is back on, catching up for the time it was powered off
Prevents the timer from ever being disabled
Makes the timer run twice as often
Keeps the timer's log messages even after a reboot
questions.explain: Persistent=true tracks whether a scheduled run was missed while the system was off and executes it as soon as the system is available again.

questions.q: Why is -rwxrwxrwx root root on a script called from root's crontab a real security risk?
options: Any unprivileged user can edit the world-writable script, and root will execute their changes the next time it runs — a privilege-escalation path
It means the script will fail to run at all
It means the script is too large for cron to execute
It has no security impact since root owns the file
questions.explain: Ownership by root doesn't matter if the permission bits still let anyone edit the file — root will run whatever content is there at the scheduled time.

questions.q: What chmod command would fix a root-owned scheduled script that is currently mode 777?
options: chmod 750 (or 700) — root-owned, not writable by group or other
chmod 777 again, since root already owns it
chmod 000, which would also prevent root from running it
chmod 644, since scripts don't need execute permission
questions.explain: Removing write access for group and other closes the privilege-escalation path while leaving root able to read, write, and execute the script.
